variants.name: CancellationTokenSource and CancellationToken
variants.implementation_notes: Cancellation is part of the .NET contract rather than an add-on: CancellationTokenSource owns the request, CancellationToken is a cheap struct passed by convention as the last parameter, and the platform's own APIs (Task.Run, Task.Delay, channel and IAsyncEnumerable overloads, ASP.NET Core request aborts) accept it. ThrowIfCancellationRequested() raises OperationCanceledException carrying that token, which is what makes an awaited task transition to TaskStatus.Canceled instead of Faulted; poll IsCancellationRequested when cleanup must run before throwing, and use token.Register(...) to bridge APIs that do not take a token. The source is one-shot and disposable, and registrations must be released.
pitfalls: Cancellation is cooperative: Cancel() does not interrupt running code. The token passed to Task.Run only prevents a not-yet-started task from running; a delegate that never observes the token runs to completion.

Catching OperationCanceledException in a broad catch (or swallowing it) breaks the task's Canceled state and hides the cancellation from the caller - rethrow it, or use an exception filter that matches the token.
CancellationTokenSource is one-shot and IDisposable: not disposing it leaks registered callbacks and timers, and calling Cancel() again after cancellation is a no-op rather than a reset.

A token that is never checked gives no cancellation latency, and locking/blocking work that ignores the token (a synchronous call in an async method) will not stop; pass the token into every blocking API that accepts one.

variants.name: Linked tokens for caller plus timeout
variants.implementation_notes: Production components usually need two triggers - the caller's cancellation and their own timeout - and .NET composes them instead of choosing: create a timeout source, link it with the caller's token via CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource and pass the linked token to the operation; CancelAfter enforces a deadline on a source you own. When the goal is only to stop waiting without stopping the underlying work, Task.WaitAsync(timeout, token) is the precise tool, because it raises TimeoutException/OperationCanceledException for the wait while the work continues. Dispose every source you create, in the right order, so registrations and timers are released promptly.
pitfalls: Forgetting to dispose the timeout or linked source leaves timers and registrations alive for the life of the source, and linking a source whose lifetime outlives the operation keeps the whole chain rooted.
A linked token cannot be reset: once either parent fires, the linked source stays cancelled, so create a fresh link per operation rather than caching one.
WaitAsync stops the wait, not the work - without a linked token the underlying operation keeps running after the timeout, which is a leak unless it is deliberately fire-and-forget.
Disposal order matters: dispose the linked source before the timeout source that feeds it, and never dispose a token source owned by the caller.
